title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn workflow control with dependencies
Skill:

Using exit status values
Conditional statements

Why:

Avoid rebuilding existing files: increases workflow speed, decreases CPU time
Control/account for different situations (multiple tasks, data types)
Validate output to avoid downstream errors

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Exit Status




Every command returns an exit status
Held on special variable $?
0: command was successful
>0: command was unsuccessful

Each number has specific meaning





echo hi
echo $?
asdf
echo $?

hi
0
bash: line 2: asdf: command not found
127

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Use Exit Status




Special commands && and || evaluate $?
&& listens for exit status 0

if 0 (success) then process continues

|| listens for exit status >0

if >0 (fail) the process continues

Can be combined
Keep these simple!




echo hi && echo pass || echo fail
asdf && echo pass || echo fail

hi
pass
bash: line 1: asdf: command not found
fail

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Square Braces




Square braces ‘[]’ evaluate an internal statement to set exit status
Internal exit status 0: external exit status 0
Internal exit status >0: external exit status 1
White space (spaces) is very important!




[ 1 == 1 ] && echo true || echo false
[ 1 == 2 ] && echo true || echo false
[ a == a ] && echo pass $? || echo fail $?
[ a == b ] && echo pass $? || echo fail $?

true
false
pass 0
fail 1

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: if




Conditional syntax utilize square braces for workflow control

i.e. execute commands only if a condition is met

Syntax structure:

if [ assertion ]
New line then
Commands
New line fi to close conditional

Conditional work only executed if exit status = 0




if [ 1 == 1 ]; then
    echo Yay
fi
if [ 1 == 2 ]; then
    echo Nay
fi

Yay




Why is == used and not =?

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: elif




Ability to capture workflow if first conditional fails
elif (else if) assessed only when if exit status = 1
An entire new conditional is written
Read conditionals top -> bottom
Multiple elif statements allowed




foo=bat
if [ $foo == bar ]; then
    echo foobar
elif [ $foo == baz ]; then
    echo foobaz
elif [ $foo == bat ]; then
    echo foobat
fi

foobat




How many conditionals failed?
What if foo=baz?

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: else




else catches all failed conditions
Specified last
Does not evaluate an assertion




foo=foo
if [ $foo == bar ]; then
    echo foobar
elif [ $foo == baz ]; then
    echo foobaz
elif [ $foo == bat ]; then
    echo foobat
else
    echo "Unrecognized value of foo"
fi

Unrecognized value of foo

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: and




Multiple assertions can be combined with &&
As before, && only continues if exit status = 0

So, all conditionals would need to be true





foo=bar
num=1
if [ $foo == bar ] && [ $num == 1 ]; then
    echo Success
fi

Success




Would [ $num == 1 ] be assessed if foo=baz?

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: or




Assertions can also be combined with ||
As before, || only continues if exit status >0

So, only one of the assertions needs to be true

These can be combined with &&




alpha=a
num=1
if [ $alpha == b ] || [ $num == 1 ]; then
    echo Success
fi

Success




If the assertion was written [ $alpha == a ], would [ $num == 1 ] have been assessed?
Which of the assertions triggers the conditional in:




[ 1 == 2 ] && [ a == a ] || [ b == b ]

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Conditionals: not




The character ! inverts logic
[ 1 != 0 ]: true ($?=0)
[ ! 1 == 0 ]: true ($?=0)
Note the white space in the second assertion
Useful to name variables to help reader through logic




[ a != b ] && echo $?
[ ! foo == bar ] && echo $?

0
0




What is printed in:




[ ! foo == bar ] && echo alpha \
    || echo beta
[ foo == bar ] || [ ! 1 == 2 ] \
    && echo delta || echo gamma

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Comparing integers




A set of special comparators operators for integers

-gt: greater than
-lt: less than
-ge: greater than or equal
-le: less than or equal
-eq: equal
-ne: not equal

Note: double parentheses are used for mathematic expressions (>, <, <=, etc)

(( 1 <= 2 ))

See more details here




[ 1 -lt 2 ] && echo 1 $?
[ ! 1 -gt 2 ] && echo 2 $?
[ 1 -le 2 ] && echo 3 $?
[ ! 1 -ge 2 ] && echo 4 $?

1 0
2 0
3 0
4 0




What is printed in:




[ ! 1 -lt 2 ] && [ 1 -eq 1 ] \
    && echo alpha || echo beta
[ 1 -gt 2 ] || [ ! 1 -ge 2 ] \
    && echo delta || echo gamma

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
File management




A set of special comparators operators for managing files

-e: something exists
-d: a directory exists
-f: a file exists
-s: a file contains data
-z: a variable is empty





[ -f foo.txt ]
[ -e foobar ]
[ -d my_dir ]
[ -z $foo ]



What is printed in:




echo "foo" > my_file.txt
[ ! -s my_file.txt ] \
    && echo alpha || echo beta

title: Conditionals: Exit status, square braces, special checks
text:
Best practices




Keep conditionals below 3 levels of logic:

Simple, flat, short

Consider breaking up long chains into multiple statements
Inverting logic often simplifies
Name variables to help through logic

is_empty: holds boolean of whether file is empty
file_exists: holds boolean of whether file exists





# Flight control with variable
foo=""
foo_empty=$([ -z $foo ] && echo $? || echo $?)
[ $foo_empty == 0 ] && echo set_var || echo move_on

# Flight control with file
touch foo.txt
foo_exists=$([ -f foo.txt ] && echo $? || echo $?)
[ $foo_exists == 0 ] && echo move_on || echo make_foo


What would be printed in the examples above?

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Build loops and nested loops
Skill:

Anatomy of for loop
Thinking in iterations
Nesting logic

Why:

Apply same set of commands multiple times
e.g. pipeline step for each subject

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
What is a For Loop




Purpose of computing: get computers to do the work
Computers are great at repeating work

Same command for different variables
Same workflow for different subjects

Benefits: replicability, efficiency, reduce programmer typing
For loops: special syntax to repeat series of commands
Nate’s Adage: Be clever

If repeating work, get computer to do it
Not lazy, efficient (without tendonitis)!









flowchart TB
  A[Start of list] --> B(Execute commands)
  B --> C{End of list?}
  C --> A
  C --> D[Exit]

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Anatomy of For Loops




For loops have a specific structure:

Space separated ‘for variable in list’
New line do, series of commands
Reference variable with $
New line done

Functionally:

Iterate through all items of list
Define variable from list for each iteration
Execute commands between do and done for each iteration





for var in {1..3}; do
    echo $var
done

1
2
3

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Iterating through lists




Possible to store lists

Use space between items
Account for bash returning space-separated output

Reference list in for loop syntax by variable
Best practices:

Add do to for loop definition line

“;” indicates End Of Line (EOL)

Indent to show logic levels
done on separate line, original indentation





my_sent="i am great"
num_list=$(echo {1..3})
# file_list=$(ls .)
for var in $my_sent $num_list; do
    echo $var
done

i
am
great
1
2
3

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
Nesting For Loops




A child loop can exist within a parent loop
Entire child loop executed for each parent loop iteration




for num in {1..3}; do
    for alpha in {a..c}; do
        echo ${num}$alpha
    done
done

1a
1b
1c
2a
2b
2c
3a
3b
3c

title: For Loops: Iterations and Nesting
text:
More Best Practices




Flatter is better

Limit nesting (logic) depth to ~3 levels
Try restructuring if deeper logic is needed
Be more clever

Organize code into blocks
Have meaningful variable names

for i in {a..c} ... vs
for alpha in {a..c} ...





for num in {1..2}; do
    for alpha in {a..b}; do
        echo ${num}$alpha
    done
done
echo
for num_alpha in {1..2}{a..b}; do
    echo $num_alpha
done

1a
1b
2a
2b

1a
1b
2a
2b

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Purpose


Knowledge:

Orient to command line interface (CLI)
Anatomy of commands
Directory structures

Skill: learn basic commands and build directory trees
Why:

CLI is the most common interface with neuroimaging software
Neuroimaging software requires certain directory structures
Thinking in trees will help organize your data

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
What is a terminal






Application - provides access to the command shell
Default language - Bourne Again Shell (Bash)
Provide instruction to computer
Useful for:

Automation
Triggering software

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Anatomy of commands




Command: instruction to machine

Matches executable in PATH
Composed of arguments
Separated by spaces

Types of Arguments:

Option: modify command, specified with flag “-”
Parameter: provides information to command or option

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Foundational commands




pwd: print working directory
ls: list directory contents

ls -l: list with extra info
ls -a: list all files
ls -la: combine arguments

cd: change directories

cd foo: go down into foo
cd ..: go up one level
cd: go HOME

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Directory tree




Every file has a path
Separate steps of path with “/”
Top of path: “root”, OS essentials
Center: “~”, HOME, default
Below HOME: user files

title: The Terminal: Linux Tree, Commands, Making directories
text:
Make directories




mkdir: creates directory, requires parameter

mkdir foo: create directory “foo”

Many available options:

mkdir -p foo/bar: create directory “bar” within “foo” (and “foo” if it does not exist)
See more options with man mkdir

use down arrow to scroll
use “q” to exit manual


tree: see directory tree structure

Mac users: install with brew install tree

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Purpose


Knowledge:

Learn how to store data for future use
Manipulate return values

Skill:

Strings and variables
Brace expansion
Manipulating variable information

Why:

Useful for building organized directory trees, file names
Commonly desirous to extract information from file name

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Strings




Series of key strokes:

abcd1234
Hello World

Good to avoid spaces (command: argument + parameter)

Hello_World

Data type - integer, boolean, list, array
Store in a variable
Access with $ prefix

Print value of variable with echo





foo="Hello World"
echo foo
echo $foo

bar=Goodbye Sky
echo $bar

foo
Hello World
bash: line 4: Sky: command not found




Why does bar=Goodbye Sky break?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Paths




File paths can be stored in variable
Two types:

Relative - start current location
Absolute - start at root

Special path: PATH

Search path of executables
Reveal command path with which

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Brace expansion




Curly braces containing a list: ‘{1..4}’
Expand sequential or comma-separated lists
Append to strings - easy file, directory generation

E.g. ‘mkdir -p sub-{1..3}’

Combine to generate permutations

E.g. ‘for i in pref-{1..3}{a..c}; do ...’

Supports nesting
Run in subshell ‘$()’ to store in variable




echo {a..d}
echo sub-{1..3}
perm=$(echo {1..3}{a..c})
nest=$(echo pref-{foo,bar{1..3},baz})
echo $perm
echo $nest

a b c d
sub-1 sub-2 sub-3
1a 1b 1c 2a 2b 2c 3a 3b 3c
pref-foo pref-bar1 pref-bar2 pref-bar3 pref-baz

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Combining variables




Access variables with ‘$’
Combine with curly braces to:

Add suff/prefix:

‘var=foo; echo ${var}bar’

Combine variables

‘var1=foo; var2=bar; echo ${var1}$var2’

Note: reuse of ‘{}’ - key-bindings are context dependent!





var1=foo; var2=bar
echo "1 ${var1}baz"
echo "2 ${var1}$var2"
echo "3 $var1$var2"
echo "4 $var1baz"

1 foobaz
2 foobar
3 foobar
4 




Why does ‘echo "4 $var1baz"’ break?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: forward removal




Often desirable to slice strings

E.g. extract “awesome” from “I_am_awesome”

Extracting subject, session, or task from file name

BIDS: sub-1_ses-A_task-memory

Combine “#” and string with variable call to slice from string beginning

“#” removes before first string match
Wildcard symbol “*” matches anything
“##” removes before final string match





bids_name=sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
echo $bids_name
echo ${bids_name#*_}
echo ${bids_name##*_}

sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
ses-A_task-memory
task-memory




What would ‘echo ${bids_name#*-}’ say?
How about ‘echo ${bids_name#sub-1}’?
How about ‘echo ${bids_name##*-}’?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: backward removal




The “%” is used to slice from the back

“%” removes after last string match
“%%” removes after first string match

An intermediate variable can be used to extract string middle




bids_name=sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
echo $bids_name
echo ${bids_name%_*}
echo ${bids_name%%_*}
int=${bids_name#*_}
echo ${int%_*}

sub-1_ses-A_task-memory
sub-1_ses-A
sub-1
ses-A

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: positional




Each character in a string has a position

0-indexed, abcd = 0123

Use “:” to specify start and end of positions




alpha="abcdefg"
echo ${alpha:0:3}
echo ${alpha:3}

abc
defg




What would ‘echo ${alpha:1:4}’ say?
What would ‘echo ${alpha:5}’ say?

title: Variables: Strings, Braces, Slicing
text:
Slice: replace




Replacing substring is possible with /
Must match substring exactly
Can also be used to remove string




foo="foobbb"
echo $foo
echo "${foo/bbb/ccc}"

foobbb
fooccc




What would ‘echo "${foo/bbb/}"’ say?

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn to save and execute work
Skill:

Write scripts and manage permissions
Execute in desired shell

Why:

Workflow replicability, transparency
Increase complexity of commands while decreasing researcher effort

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Scripts




Enter commands into terminal:

Fine for few, short commands
Many - tedious, error prone

Scripting:

Save commands into file (script)
Execute file

Utility:

Reusable scripts
Error checking
Decrease typing

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Create New Script




touch: Create new file

Update write-time for existing files

nano: Create and open file with built-in editor

Other built-ins: vi, vim, emacs
Exit sequence:

ctrl-x: save and exit
y: overwrite
specify name, return


Specify interpreter via #!

Provides path to executable

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
CHMOD




CHange MODe of files
ls -l shows file permissions by group

User, group, other

Numeric access (8 bit):

read (4), write (2), execute (1)
rw- = 6
rwxr-xr-x = 755

chmod 755 new_script.sh - detail permission for each group
chmod +x new_script.sh - assign execute to all groups

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Execution




Execute in different shells

current vs sub shell

Relevant for variable availability
Method 1: source or dot execution

source new_script.sh
. new_script.sh is preferred
Executes script in current shell
Variables available for future use
Ideal for creating environments
Overrides permissions (discouraged)

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Execution, cont’d




Method 2: direct execution

./new_script.sh
Executes script in sub-shell
Variables only exist in sub-shell
Ideal for executing independent scripts

Method 3: interpreter execution

bash new_script.sh
Executes script in specified shell
Discouraged, specify interpreter in script

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
IDEs




Integrated Development Environments
Editor: syntax highlighting, formatting, error detection
Compiler or Interpreter: build and execute
Extra features:

Testing
Debugging
Visualization
Remote Development

Popular for Bash

Sublime: simple text editor, “free”
VS Code: IDE, plugins for languages, free for research and learning

title: Scripting: Permissions, Shells, and IDEs
text:
Style guides


Individual programming style - “Spaghetti Code”

Difficult to read, maintain, optimize
xkcd comic

Strongly encourage using style guides

Google Style

Reasons:

Increases professionalism
Ability to collaborate
Access to plugins (autoformatter, linter, documentation)
Program faster
Reduce learning curve

title: For Loops: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Purpose


Knowledge: Learn to align information across lists and build flexible for loops
Skill:

Arrays and counters
Control number of iterations

Why:

Linking information (e.g. label-anatomy)
Decrease workflow time and number of errors

title: For Loops: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
C-style for loop




Bash supports another for loop specification:

Specify start, final, and increment values
Using numerical assessment parentheses (double)
Separated by semicolon

Only works with integers




for ((i=1; i<5; i++)); do
    echo $i
done

1
2
3
4

title: For Loops: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Dynamic iteration control




Start and final values do not have to be hardcoded
C-style supports referencing a variable
These start and final variables could be set by another process

num_foo=$(ls foo*.txt | wc -l)





start=1
end=5
for ((i=$start; i<$end; i++)); do
    echo $i
done

1
2
3
4

title: For Loops: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
While loops and counters




While loops can also be used to control iteration number
Syntax based on an assertion being true
Specific structure:

Space separated while [ assertion ]
New line do
Series of commands
Typically a variable is updated
New line done





cnt=1
while [ $cnt -lt 5 ]; do
    echo $cnt
    let cnt+=1
done

1
2
3
4

title: For Loops: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Arrays




Arrays are a 0-indexed data type
Positional structure:

Defined within parentheses
Space separated

Data extracted by referencing position




arr_foo=({a..d})
arr_fruit=(apple orange banana)
echo ${arr_foo[0]}
echo ${arr_fruit[2]}

a
banana




Why was ${arr_fruit[2]} used and not ${arr_fruit[3]}?

title: For Loops: Arrays, counters, dynamic control
text:
Arrays: length




Special syntax to extract array length

${#arr[@]}
# queries length

Useful for extracting positions from multiple arrays




hero=(batman superman aquaman)
color=(black red green)
echo "hero array length is ${#hero[@]}"

# Check arrays are same length
[ ${#hero[@]} == ${#color[@]} ] \
    || echo "Array length mismatch"

idx=0
while [ $idx -lt ${#hero[@]} ]; do
    echo "The hero ${hero[$idx]} wears ${color[$idx]}"
    let idx+=1

Arrays: position




Special syntax to reference array indices

${!arr[@]}
! queries indices
@ references all array values

Useful for iterations through array positions




arr=({a..d})
echo "Array positions are ${!arr[@]}"

for pos in ${!arr[@]}; do
    echo "Array position $pos value is ${arr[$pos]}"
done

Array positions are 0 1 2 3
Array position 0 value is a
Array position 1 value is b
Array position 2 value is c
Array position 3 value is d

Building arrays and variables




Variables and arrays can be built
Operator += allows for concatentation

In addition to increasing integer values

Command unset clears variables




unset var_foo
unset arr_foo

[ -z var_foo ] && echo empty

for i in {1..4}; do
    var_foo+="$i"
    arr_foo+=($i)
done

[ -z var_foo ] || echo full

echo $var_foo
echo ${var_foo[@]}
